File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 9 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to slip a backdoor into a widely used software development kit for the Injective blockchain. Disguised as harmless analytics, the code quietly captured wallet recovery phrases and private keys and sent them to an attacker-controlled server the moment a wallet was created or loaded. Automatic publishing pushed the tainted code out to 18 related packages within minutes, and it stayed live for less than an hour before being pulled and fixed. If your application installed any of the affected packages during that window, or pic…

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 payload file dropped on disk · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Injective SDK wallet-key exfil to lookalike domain testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Injective SDK wallet-key exfil to lookalike domain testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound resolution/connection to the attacker-controlled exfil host that the backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 reassembles from an obfuscated char-code array and POSTs stolen seed phrases / private keys to (carried base64 in the X-Request-Id header). The FQDN is a lookalike of legitimate Injective gRPC-Web infra but is not a real Injective endpoint, so exact-host contact is high fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the exact FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network decoded from the char-code array (_e/_d) in key-derivation-telemetry.ts; cross-checked against BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and SlowMist which all cite this host as the POST destination for the base64 secret in the X-Request-Id header. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html • https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-injective-sdk-compromised-crypto-wallet-private-keys-stolen-0b8f06bf37ad • https://crypto.news/compromised-injective-sdk-sends-wallet-keys-through-fake-telemetry/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI runner still on the backdoored 1.20.21 build genuinely beaconing (this is a true positive, not an FP)
  • Malware sandbox / detonation VM replaying the sample and resolving the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner or DNS sinkhole appliance resolving the indicator during enrichment
  • Security researcher manually curling the host to confirm it is live
Suppression filter
// scope to the SDK runtime to drop scanner/appliance noise
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","electron.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the initiating process (expect node.exe/electron.exe or a browser running a wallet/DEX frontend); pull the app's package-lock/node_modules to confirm @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 is present. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and force-rotate every wallet seed phrase and private key that host touched — treat all as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for the malicious file (key-derivation-telemetry / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js), sweep the fleet for other hosts resolving the domain, and audit any downstream package pinning 1.20.21.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl =~ "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name =~ "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode = ResultCodeName, ResolvedIPs = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 payload file dropped on disk AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the tainted SDK landing in node_modules on developer workstations, build agents, or servers via the distinctive payload filenames (key-derivation-telemetry.ts/.js, dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) and the two published SHA256 hashes. These artifacts do not exist in the clean SDK, making on-disk presence unambiguous evidence of the compromised 1.20.21 release. Rationale: Uses the payload filenames from Stage 2 (key-derivation-telemetry.ts and compiled dist/esm/accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) plus the two article-published SHA256 hashes — none of which exist in the clean 1.20.23 build — so any hit is a direct indicator of the tainted release rather than a behavioural heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html • https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-injective-sdk-compromised-crypto-wallet-private-keys-stolen-0b8f06bf37ad
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security tooling (Socket, Snyk, Ox Security) storing a quarantined/sample copy of the malicious file for analysis
  • A malware analyst manually saving the IOC file to a case folder
  • Backup or artifact-cache restore replaying an old node_modules tree containing 1.20.21
  • An unrelated project coincidentally shipping a benign file named key-derivation-telemetry.js (hash mismatch distinguishes it)
Suppression filter
// drop AV/EDR quarantine and analyst sample copies
| where FolderPath !contains "Quarantine" and FolderPath !contains "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\samples"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FolderPath sits under node_modules/@injectivelabs and check whether SHA256 matches a published hash; identify the writing process (npm/pnpm/yarn/node) and the account. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the tainted package, force reinstall of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.23+ with a fresh lockfile, and clear npm/pnpm caches on the host and shared CI cache. 3) Hunt: rotate every wallet seed/private key any app on that host derived while 1.20.21 was resident, then sweep the fleet and build agents for the same filenames/hashes and for outbound contact to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("key-derivation-telemetry.ts","key-derivation-telemetry.js","accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
    or SHA256 in ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0","9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("key-derivation-telemetry.ts","key-derivation-telemetry.js","accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
    or TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0","9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) · [LLM] TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) · [LLM] Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) · [LLM] CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain)
Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the hardcoded self-propagating payload files the Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon npm worm drops during a malicious package preinstall, matched by exact filename and known SHA256. The article cites Sha1-Hulud dumping harvested credentials into public GitHub repos as the exfiltration destination it warns about; this catches the worm at the execution stage before that exfil happens. Rationale: Uses the exact worm payload filenames (setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) and four published SHA256 hashes from Datadog/Microsoft analyses of Sha1-Hulud 2.0 — the campaign the article names as the archetype of GitHub-hosted secret exfiltration. Filename+hash makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a captured Sha1-Hulud sample in a sandbox VONM
  • Threat-intel/malware-repo mirror syncing sample files to a scanning host
  • EDR test/purple-team exercise seeding the named hashes
  • A benign project legitimately shipping a file literally named setup_bun.js (rare; hash filter avoids this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareSamples\\","\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 matches a known worm hash and identify the InitiatingProcess (should be node/npm/bun preinstall). Pull the parent package name and package.json to find the poisoned dependency. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner, revoke any npm/GitHub/cloud tokens present on it, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same hashes and for any public GitHub repos with description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.'; rotate every secret reachable from the affected build.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a JavaScript package-manager process (node, npm, bun, yarn, pnpm) reaching the cloud instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal) — the multi-cloud credential-harvest step of the Sha1-Hulud worm. This is the 'secret theft that never touches github.com' the article says public monitoring cannot see. Rationale: Combines the concrete IMDS endpoints (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) documented by Datadog/Unit42 with the JS package-manager parent context that distinguishes worm harvesting from a legitimate cloud SDK call. Pins the abuse to the install-time process rather than any app. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js application running on an EC2/GCE instance that legitimately queries IMDS via the AWS/GCP SDK
  • Serverless/build tooling (e.g. serverless-framework, terraform-node wrappers) resolving instance credentials
  • Cloud-native CI agents written in Node fetching a metadata-scoped token for artifact upload
  • IMDSv2 token-refresh loops from a long-running node service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall","ci","npx") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the node/bun process was part of an npm/yarn install lifecycle (check parent chain and recent package.json changes) versus a steady-state application. Install-time IMDS access is the true positive. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the instance role's temporary credentials, quarantine the runner/host, and enforce IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 to block the container reach. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js, trufflehog execution, and any subsequent api.github.com repo creation; rotate cloud keys the role could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the TruffleHog secret-discovery binary launched as a child of a JavaScript package manager or a shell inside an install script — the on-disk credential-sweep stage of the Sha1-Hulud worm. Distinct from sanctioned CI secret-scanning because the parent is node/npm/bun rather than a dedicated scanner job. Rationale: TruffleHog execution parented by node/bun/npm is the documented Sha1-Hulud secret-discovery step (Datadog/Wiz). The parent-process predicate separates worm-driven scans from an intentional trufflehog CI stage, keeping fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately runs trufflehog as a pre-commit/secret-scan step invoked from an npm script
  • Developer running `npx trufflehog` manually to audit a repo
  • Security tooling wrappers that shell out to trufflehog from a Node orchestrator
  • pre-commit framework invoking trufflehog via a node hook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","secret-scan","security-scan","gitleaks-trufflehog-step"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm trufflehog was not a sanctioned pipeline step — inspect the initiating package.json script and whether the run coincides with an npm install rather than a scan job. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and revoke tokens; if part of a build, halt the pipeline and quarantine produced artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with IMDS access, bun payload files, and outbound api.github.com repo creation on the same host; rotate any secrets trufflehog could have read.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","npm.cmd","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm registering an attacker-controlled self-hosted GitHub Actions runner — identified by the runner name SHA1HULUD, the $HOME/.dev-env install directory, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, and the actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0 download. This is the worm turning GitHub into a persistence/C2 channel, exactly the github.com-as-infrastructure abuse the article describes. Rationale: Pins on four hard, campaign-unique strings from Datadog's Sha1-Hulud 2.0 analysis (runner name SHA1HULUD, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, ~/.dev-env, actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0). These do not appear in legitimate runner setups, giving alerting-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An org that coincidentally uses a self-hosted runner directory named .dev-env (unlikely, and runner-name string still filters it)
  • Admin legitimately setting RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1 in a container runner build (would lack the SHA1HULUD name)
  • Runner version 2.330.0 downloaded during a legitimate GitHub-hosted runner upgrade (string paired with the other markers reduces this)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the runner registration name is SHA1HULUD or the install path is $HOME/.dev-env; check which GitHub org/repo the runner registered against. Step 2 (contain): Remove the runner from GitHub org settings, kill the runner process, revoke the PAT/GITHUB_TOKEN it used, and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Search GitHub audit logs for self-hosted runner additions and for workflows triggered `on: discussion` with a `runs-on: self-hosted` job echoing github.event.discussion.body; enumerate other hosts with .dev-env.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm's destructive fallback that fires when it cannot authenticate/propagate: on Windows `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%` plus `cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, and on Linux `find $HOME ... | xargs shred -uvz`. High-impact, low-frequency behaviour that turns a supply-chain compromise into data destruction. Rationale: Encodes the exact destructive commands Datadog documented for Sha1-Hulud's failure path (`cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%*`, `find $HOME ... shred -uvz`). cipher /W over a user profile and shred over $HOME are near-zero in normal ops, making impact-stage alerting reliable. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/GPO running `cipher /W:` to wipe free space during decommissioning (usually not scoped to %USERPROFILE% and not spawned by node)
  • Backup or forensics tooling using shred for secure deletion of scratch data
  • A cleanup script using recursive del on a temp path (USERPROFILE token filter reduces this)
  • Disk-sanitisation compliance jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","sh","bash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName =~ "cipher.exe"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the parent process — a wipe parented by node/bun/sh during an npm install is the true positive; capture the exact target path. Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from the network to stop further destruction and preserve volume shadow copies/backups; snapshot the disk. Step 3 (hunt): Confirm the Sha1-Hulud chain (bun payloads, trufflehog, IMDS, SHA1HULUD runner) on the host and across the fleet; initiate restore-from-backup and org-wide secret rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cipher.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "cipher.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a package-manager process reaching cloud IMDS with the same host contacting api.github.com/github.com within 30 minutes — the Sha1-Hulud pattern of harvesting cloud secrets then pushing them into a newly created public GitHub repo. This directly targets the 'close the exfiltration gap' thesis of the article: catching secrets leaving CI toward github.com, not after they surface. Rationale: Chains the two documented Sha1-Hulud network behaviours (IMDS credential harvest → push to a new github.com repo) on the same host within a tight window, which is far more specific than either signal alone and maps precisely to the article's exfiltration-to-github concern. Time-window correlation makes it a hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node app on a cloud VM that reads IMDS and also pushes to GitHub (e.g. a release bot / GitOps agent) within the window
  • CI runner that legitimately fetches instance credentials then interacts with the GitHub API for status checks
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation touching both IMDS and github.com
  • Container build that queries metadata for a token and pushes an image manifest referencing github.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall") or RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the github.com interaction — was a NEW repo created (check GitHub audit log for repo.create with an 18-char hex name or description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.')? Confirm the IMDS call was install-time. Step 2 (contain): Delete the attacker repo, revoke the developer's GitHub token and the instance role credentials, and isolate the host/runner. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for bun payload files, trufflehog, and the SHA1HULUD runner on the host; enumerate all public repos org-wide matching the campaign description and rotate every exposed secret.
let LookbackDays = 30d;

    | project ImdsTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, HarvestProc = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","git","git.exe","curl","curl.exe")
| join kind=inner Imds on DeviceId

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, ImdsTime, HarvestProc, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ImdsTime)
| order by Timestamp desc

Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 16 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The jscrambler npm package was compromised, and simply installing its&nbsp;8.14.0&nbsp;release runs an infostealer on your machine. Published on July 11, 2026, the malicious version carries a&nbsp;preinstall&nbsp;hook that drops and executes a native binary, one build each for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Socket flagged the release&nbsp;six minutes after it was published. If you or one of your

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install
Installation. Command & Control. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud instance-metadata (IMDS) harvest by temp-dropped / Node-spawned process · [LLM] Credential / browser / wallet / AI-tool config theft by temp-dropped process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
jscrambler@8.14.0 npm package acquisition (compromised release) AIDelivery High
Hunts install/CI processes that request the trojanised jscrambler 8.14.0 release named in the article. Any acquisition of this exact version inside the vulnerable window is an initial-access indicator because the release ships a preinstall hook that runs an infostealer. Rationale: Uses the article's exact malicious identifier jscrambler@8.14.0; the token pair 'jscrambler'+'8.14.0' on an npm/node command line is high-fidelity because 8.15.0/8.13.0 are the clean versions to move to. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally pinning 8.14.0 in a sandbox to analyse the payload
  • Lockfile audit tooling echoing the string 'jscrambler@8.14.0' while remediating (grep/npm ls output captured as a command line)
  • A developer typing the version in a shell to check whether it is installed
  • SBOM/vuln scanners printing the affected version in scan output
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm ls" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm audit" and ProcessCommandLine !has "audit"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the command actually installed (exit code / node_modules write) versus merely referenced the string in an audit; capture host, user, timestamp. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove jscrambler@8.14.0 from lockfiles/caches and repin to 8.15.0 or 8.13.0, and treat any secret reachable by the install context as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for a temp-dir binary spawned by node.exe and outbound traffic to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 within seconds of install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","node.exe","npx.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","yarn.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.cmd","node.exe"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jscrambler" and ProcessCommandLine has "8.14.0"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "jscrambler" and CommandLine has "8.14.0"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: jscrambler 8.14.0 compromised npm package acquisition
id: 5f1c8a12-3d6b-4b21-9a7e-0c1f9e2a4b01
description: Detects install/CI processes requesting the trojanised jscrambler@8.14.0 release
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'jscrambler'
      - '8.14.0'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@CommandLine:*jscrambler* AND @CommandLine:*8.14.0*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/jscrambler/i
| CommandLine=/8\.14\.0/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","node.exe","npx.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","yarn.cmd") OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("npm.cmd","node.exe")) (Processes.process="*jscrambler*" Processes.process="*8.14.0*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","node.exe","npx.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","yarn.cmd") OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("npm.cmd","node.exe")) (Processes.process="*jscrambler*" Processes.process="*8.14.0*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Rust infostealer binary dropped and run detached from npm preinstall hook AIInstallation High
Detects the setup.js loader behaviour: node.exe writing a randomly-named executable to the system temp directory and launching it detached. Anchors on the parent=node/npm + child-in-temp lineage and on the article's payload SHA-256 hashes. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's loader chain (setup.js drops a random-named temp binary and launches it detached) plus the three confirmed payload SHA-256 hashes; parent=node + child-in-temp is the fixed structural signal that survives the randomised filename. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog • https://safedep.io
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit npm postinstall of packages that compile/extract native addons to temp (node-gyp, esbuild, sharp prebuild)
  • Electron/VS Code extension installers unpacking helpers to temp via node
  • Playwright/Puppeteer downloading browser binaries into a cache under temp
  • Corporate build agents running node-based codegen that stages executables in temp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","playwright","puppeteer","electron") and SHA256 !in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child SHA-256 and compare against the three payload hashes; if unmatched, hash-lookup in VT and inspect whether the file is hidden (leading dot) and launched with hidden output. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host, quarantine the temp binary, and remove jscrambler@8.14.0. 3) Hunt: check for the persistence artefacts (hidden per-minute scheduled task / LaunchAgent) and outbound C2 to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/")
   or FileName startswith "."
   or SHA256 in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has "node.exe" or ParentProcessName has "npm"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloud instance-metadata (IMDS) harvest by temp-dropped / Node-spawned process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts connections to the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254 / metadata.google.internal) initiated by node or a temp-dropped process, matching the article's claim that the stealer scrapes the metadata endpoints CI runners use for AWS/Azure/GCP credentials. Rationale: 169.254.169.254 is the fixed link-local IMDS address; the article explicitly calls out harvesting of the metadata endpoints CI runners use, and constraining the initiator to node/temp separates the stealer from legitimate cloud SDK usage. Sentinel path drops process context because ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process column. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit AWS/GCP SDK calls to IMDS from a Node app running on an EC2/GCE instance
  • CI runner agents refreshing instance-role credentials via node tooling
  • Cloud-init / metadata polling by monitoring agents packaged as node processes
  • kube2iam / instance-role sidecars proxying metadata
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "server.js" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is the randomly-named temp binary (not the app's own node server) and whether an IMDSv2 token flow or raw v1 GET was used; note the host's cloud role. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate the instance-role credentials and any keys the role can reach, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate with the same host's outbound C2 to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 and check CloudTrail for AssumeRole/API calls from the harvested credentials off-instance.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl in~ ("metadata.google.internal","169.254.169.254")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254" or DstHostname in~ ("metadata.google.internal")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Credential / browser / wallet / AI-tool config theft by temp-dropped process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a temp-located or node-spawned process touching the exact secret stores the article lists: browser password/cookie DBs, Bitwarden vault, MetaMask/Phantom/Exodus wallets, ~/.ssh and ~/.aws, and AI-coding-tool config dirs (Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Zed) holding API keys and MCP credentials. Rationale: Every path in the selection is named explicitly by the article's target list (AWS/Azure/GCP creds, MetaMask/Phantom/Exodus, Bitwarden, browser stores, and the AI-tool/MCP config dirs for Claude/Cursor/Windsurf/VS Code/Zed); constraining the actor to a temp/node process is what makes bulk secret-store touching an infostealer signal rather than normal app usage. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog
ATT&CKT1005 T1555.003 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The browsers/wallet apps themselves reading their own stores (excluded by actor filter, but a renamed temp copy can slip)
  • Backup or sync agents copying profile directories
  • Bitwarden/1Password native apps refreshing vault caches
  • Developer scripts run via node that legitimately read ~/.aws or ~/.ssh for deploys
  • VS Code / Cursor reading their own config on launch
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","Bitwarden.exe","Code.exe","Cursor.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the acting process is the random-named temp binary (not the owning app) and enumerate which stores were touched in the same second-window. 2) Contain: isolate host; force-revoke browser/Bitwarden/Discord/Slack sessions, rotate cloud/npm/GitHub and AI-tool/MCP API keys, and move crypto out of any wallet on the host. 3) Hunt: tie the file touches to a subsequent outbound TLS session to the C2 IPs or Tor endpoints and to the IMDS harvest UC.

| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName

ImFileEvent

Hidden per-minute scheduled task / LaunchAgent persistence by npm-dropped binary AIInstallation Medium
Detects the article's persistence step: a hidden Windows scheduled task set to relaunch every minute (or a macOS LaunchAgent), created by a temp-located or node-spawned process rather than an installer or admin. Rationale: The article specifies a hidden Windows scheduled task that relaunches every minute; a per-minute (/sc minute) schtasks /create whose parent is node/npm or a temp binary is a very tight persistence signal since near-nothing legitimately schedules per-minute relaunch from a package install. macOS LaunchAgent variant is covered via DeviceFileEvents on ~/Library/LaunchAgents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog • https://safedep.io
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1543.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit monitoring/agent installers that register frequent tasks (rare at per-minute cadence)
  • Developer tooling that self-registers a watcher task
  • RMM software deploying a heartbeat task via a node-based installer
  • Admin manually creating a per-minute task for troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("MicrosoftEdgeUpdate","GoogleUpdate","OneDrive")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task's action/command (the /tr argument) and confirm it points at a hidden temp binary; on macOS inspect the newly-written plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents. 2) Contain: delete the task/plist, kill the referenced binary, isolate the host, and remove jscrambler@8.14.0. 3) Hunt: pivot on the referenced binary's hash and outbound C2, and sweep the fleet for the same task name / plist label.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "minute"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "minute"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm") or ParentProcessName has @"\Temp\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 to jscrambler infostealer hardcoded IPs and Tor infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerting IOC match on the two attacker C2 IPs and the Tor endpoints StepSecurity observed the dropped binary reaching at runtime. Any host contacting these is treated as an active infection. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the two attacker endpoints (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) and the Tor hostnames that StepSecurity published as the first runtime network indicators for the campaign; IP-literal matches are low-FP and warrant alerting. CloudWatch omitted because this is endpoint egress telemetry, not CloudTrail management-plane data. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog • https://socket.dev/blog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A privacy-conscious user legitimately running Tor Browser hitting check.torproject.org (Tor hostnames only, not the two IPs)
  • Threat-intel sandbox / researcher deliberately detonating the sample
  • Shared-hosting reuse of 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79 for benign services after takedown
  • Security scanner validating the IOC block is effective
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect the random-named temp binary) and whether the two IP hits accompany the Tor endpoints; the IP hits alone are treated as confirmed. 2) Contain: block 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79 at egress, isolate the host, and begin credential rotation for everything the host could reach. 3) Hunt: sweep proxy/firewall/DNS logs fleet-wide for the same IPs, and pivot to the install and persistence UCs on any matching host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
   or RemoteUrl in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79") or DstHostname in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anomalous public egress from npm-spawned temp binary (post-install beacon) AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioural companion to the IOC C2 rule: surfaces a temp-located binary whose parent is node/npm making outbound public connections shortly after install, catching the stealer's beacon even when it rotates off the two known IPs. Rationale: Encodes the article's process lineage (npm preinstall -> node -> random temp binary) as the pivot and flags any public egress from that binary, so the beacon is caught even after the known IPs rotate. Sentinel left empty because ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process/parent column to express the node->temp-binary lineage this detection depends on. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog
ATT&CKT1071 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm postinstall scripts fetching remote assets via a helper binary in temp
  • node-based CLIs auto-updating from a CDN
  • Prebuild/native-addon downloaders reaching GitHub releases
  • Telemetry/analytics beacons from legit dev tooling launched by node
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","electron")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the temp binary's hash and reputation, and review the destination set/ports for beacon-like periodicity. 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate host, block the destinations, and kill the binary + its persistence task. 3) Hunt: cross-check the destinations against the two known C2 IPs and Tor endpoints and expand to other hosts that installed jscrambler@8.14.0.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","curl.exe","git.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,20), Dsts=make_set(RemoteIP,50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,20), Dsts=make_set(RemoteIP,50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc

jscrambler package tampering: unexpected setup.js/intro.js binaries under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Detects the supply-chain artefacts themselves — the two files the compromised release added under dist/ (setup.js loader and the 7.8MB intro.js binary container) landing in node_modules/jscrambler, matched by name and by the added-file SHA-256 hashes. Rationale: Anchored on the two exact files the package diff introduced (dist/setup.js and dist/intro.js) inside node_modules/jscrambler and their published SHA-256 hashes; these files exist nowhere in jscrambler's clean source, so their presence is unambiguous tampering evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog • https://safedep.io
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher extracting the malicious tarball to a repo path for analysis
  • Backup/restore replaying an infected node_modules snapshot
  • Unrelated packages that legitimately ship a setup.js/intro.js but under a different vendor path (excluded by the jscrambler path constraint)
  • Mirror/cache warming that copies the bad artefact between hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file hash matches the published setup.js/intro.js SHA-256 and locate every host/lockfile that pulled the artefact. 2) Contain: purge node_modules and npm cache, repin jscrambler to 8.15.0/8.13.0, and rebuild clean; treat any host that resolved these files as potentially detonated. 3) Hunt: on each matching host pivot to the temp-binary execution, persistence, and C2 UCs and rotate all reachable secrets.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\jscrambler\" or FolderPath has "/node_modules/jscrambler/"
| where FileName in~ ("setup.js","intro.js")
   or SHA256 in ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60","a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\jscrambler\" or TargetFilePath has "/node_modules/jscrambler/"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.js","intro.js") or TargetFileSHA256 in ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60","a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a742de963f14a92d24ebcbc7b44ac867e23a20d31d1b0094a13a4f83287f4e60", "a41a523ef9517aab37ed6eea0ec881821bdcb7aefcb5c5f603adc7907f868c86", "fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

cms_plugin.exe Rust stager execution + payload pull from 193.42.25.65 AIInstallation High
Hunts the custom 'cms_plugin.exe' implant that masqueraded as a Complaint Management System portal update on Balochistan Police infrastructure. The Rust stager variant downloads a next stage from 193.42.25.65 and prints 'Update Complete! Please refresh the page'. Fires on the named binary executing or any host reaching the stager download IP. Rationale: cms_plugin.exe is a unique implant filename and 193.42.25.65 is the confirmed Rust-stager download server named in the SentinelLABS report; both are non-generic, so a match is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked SentinelOne report and The Record write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named plugin binary in an unrelated product also called cms_plugin.exe (rare; validate hash and path)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox VM enrolled in EDR
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing 193.42.25.65 for research
  • Proxy/NAT egress IP collision where 193.42.25.65 is re-used by a benign CDN in future (validate at trigger time)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Sandbox\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("IR-SANDBOX-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the process tree, SHA256, and folder path for cms_plugin.exe; confirm parent (likely w3wp.exe/web-app service on a CMS/web server) and whether the host is an internet-facing police web application server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 193.42.25.65 at the perimeter, and preserve the binary for reversing. 3) Hunt: sweep all web servers for cms_plugin.exe uploads, search web logs on cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk-style portals for the file, and pivot on the SHA1s and the full campaign C2 IP set (see C2 UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "193.42.25.65" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cms_plugin.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\cms_plugin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, Signal="process", NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Dest=""),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "193.42.25.65"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, Account=SourceUserName, Signal="network", NewProcessName=ProcessName, CommandLine="", ParentProcessName="", Dest=DestinationIP)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Balochistan Police cms_plugin.exe Implant Execution
id: 6b1f2c9a-4d3e-4a11-9c77-2f0b8e5a1d42
description: Detects execution of the custom cms_plugin.exe implant deployed against Pakistani law enforcement (SentinelLABS).
references:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@EventID:3 @DestinationIp:193.42.25.65) OR (@EventID:1 @Image:(*\cms_plugin.exe OR *\CMS_Plugin.exe OR *\CMS_PLUGIN.EXE))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="193.42.25.65"

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="cms_plugin.exe" OR Processes.original_file_name="cms_plugin.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Fake 360Safe.exe (.NET) reflectively loading AsyncRAT AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second cms_plugin.exe variant: a .NET executable that masquerades as '360Safe.exe' (a legitimate Qihoo 360 Total Security binary) to reflectively load an in-memory AsyncRAT client. Detects a process named 360Safe.exe whose file metadata is NOT Qihoo/360 or which runs from outside the legitimate 360 install path. Rationale: The report states one implant variant masquerades specifically as 360Safe.exe (Qihoo 360) to reflectively load AsyncRAT; a 360Safe.exe binary running outside the genuine Qihoo install path (or lacking Qihoo file metadata) is a high-fidelity masquerade signal, especially in a Pakistani gov environment unlikely to run Chinese AV. Corroborated by SentinelOne report and Kaspersky's Mysterious Elephant AsyncRAT/Remcos tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://securelist.com/mysterious-elephant-apt-ttps-and-tools/117596/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Qihoo 360 Total Security installed to a non-default drive/path (validate publisher signature)
  • Portable/standalone 360 Total Security run from a USB or Downloads folder by a user
  • Software-deployment tool staging the real 360Safe.exe in a temp cache before install
  • AV bake-off / procurement testing of 360 Total Security by IT
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the digital signature and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName of the 360Safe.exe image — genuine is signed by Qihoo/360; the implant will be unsigned or mis-signed. Inspect for .NET/CLR module loads and outbound connections. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (AsyncRAT is in-memory), block associated C2 IPs. 3) Hunt: search DeviceImageLoadEvents for clr.dll/mscoree loading into 360Safe.exe, and correlate with cms_plugin.exe drops and the campaign C2 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "360Safe.exe"
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("360","Qihoo")) or FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(NewProcessName) endswith "\\360safe.exe"
| where not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files (x86)\\360\\") and not(tolower(NewProcessName) startswith "c:\\program files\\360\\")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
