Beaconing to Balochistan Police espionage C2 / stager IP set AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the confirmed command-and-control and staging IPs across the four converging clusters (Cobalt Strike C2 142.171.183.8, Rust-stager host 193.42.25.65, plus the campaign infrastructure block) targeting Pakistani law enforcement. Any internal host reaching these IPs warrants investigation. Rationale: 142.171.183.8 is the named Cobalt Strike C2 and 193.42.25.65 the stager host; the remaining IPs are the pre-extracted campaign infrastructure. These are static, second-source-consistent IOCs, so egress to any of them is high-fidelity for this specific converging-actor campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://therecord.media/china-india-ran-separate-spy-campaigns-against-same-police-force
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned to a shared hosting/CDN provider serving benign sites (re-validate WHOIS at trigger time)
  • Internal threat-intel platform or vulnerability scanner actively probing the C2 IPs
  • Security researcher pivoting on the infrastructure from a corporate egress IP
  • Firewall/proxy that logs a blocked (denied) attempt — confirm DeviceAction/outcome is allow before escalating
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt") and RemoteIPType == "Public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the InitiatingProcess making the connection; check whether the connection succeeded vs was blocked, and beacon regularity (jitter/interval). 2) Contain: block all listed IPs at the perimeter, isolate any host with a successful/repeated connection, and snapshot memory for the process (PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/AsyncRAT are memory-resident). 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash against the campaign SHA1 list, sweep for cms_plugin.exe and fake 360Safe.exe, and review the FortiMail email gateway and web-app servers for the initial foothold.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort,10) by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:

  - attack.t1105

  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp:
      - '142.171.183.8'
      - '193.42.25.65'
      - '41.216.188.140'
      - '89.31.121.220'
      - '45.125.32.218'

      - '172.111.233.12'

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:(142.171.183.8 OR 193.42.25.65 OR 41.216.188.140 OR 89.31.121.220 OR 45.125.32.218 OR 172.111.233.36 OR 172.111.233.96 OR 172.111.233.12 OR 172.111.233.105 OR 172.111.233.26 OR 172.94.9.49 OR 172.94.9.43 OR 172.94.9.19 OR 45.74.6.17)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","41.216.188.140","89.31.121.220","45.125.32.218","172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "41.216.188.140", "89.31.121.220", "45.125.32.218", "172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17") or RemoteUrl has_any ("cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "41.216.188.140", "89.31.121.220", "45.125.32.218", "172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "41.216.188.140", "89.31.121.220", "45.125.32.218", "172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("142.171.183.8", "193.42.25.65", "41.216.188.140", "89.31.121.220", "45.125.32.218", "172.111.233.36", "172.111.233.96", "172.111.233.12", "172.111.233.105", "172.111.233.26", "172.94.9.49", "172.94.9.43", "172.94.9.19", "45.74.6.17")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("cms.balochistanpolice.gov.pk")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["23f6781919a50b118d8d4e6a7e9ae63b71ecc885", "4039454c9189e64285e93fc075a30b93f814b5b5", "58cb2d95063b9df807b7aa8dc106b74ce988a491", "000fad96a85dd6933c22d3dbec9aed47b7f1f066", "08570471f39bb6725f07b8cddbea99ed48c22686", "23f4766c011d193f076dfc735dc460e2a41ead79", "47f8cb0c2dcf62702f58cfc1603d6325755f6820", "5d60ff36ff519c2e13e7f66cfa0bb46be79592a7", "63b88d00331de88af696dfb7a896935d830e485f", "8c329db96e093fa25268e078405a33c518dbb5c9", "d66ab0cd2e44dc8389c111b7ea34c7bcb0b35311", "2bab40c55637398f0497cff9c8cbea564d595c7f", "539bd79fbb684edea94eb37518134b97e94b9dd8", "6fe2e74d009abbd56de01fd7404a1245e9b47c79", "71757adba833b46f961e840d0f055bcce0b529c4", "c6c197e61079a0a33108c2c87b5e3c7056a138ec"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("23f6781919a50b118d8d4e6a7e9ae63b71ecc885", "4039454c9189e64285e93fc075a30b93f814b5b5", "58cb2d95063b9df807b7aa8dc106b74ce988a491", "000fad96a85dd6933c22d3dbec9aed47b7f1f066", "08570471f39bb6725f07b8cddbea99ed48c22686", "23f4766c011d193f076dfc735dc460e2a41ead79", "47f8cb0c2dcf62702f58cfc1603d6325755f6820", "5d60ff36ff519c2e13e7f66cfa0bb46be79592a7", "63b88d00331de88af696dfb7a896935d830e485f", "8c329db96e093fa25268e078405a33c518dbb5c9", "d66ab0cd2e44dc8389c111b7ea34c7bcb0b35311", "2bab40c55637398f0497cff9c8cbea564d595c7f", "539bd79fbb684edea94eb37518134b97e94b9dd8", "6fe2e74d009abbd56de01fd7404a1245e9b47c79", "71757adba833b46f961e840d0f055bcce0b529c4", "c6c197e61079a0a33108c2c87b5e3c7056a138ec")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Critical Zimbra Flaw Could Let Crafted Emails Run Malicious Code in User Sessions

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 11 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Zimbra is urging customers to apply updates to address a critical security vulnerability impacting the Classic Web Client that could result in arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability has been described as a case of stored cross-site scripting (XSS) that could allow specially crafted emails to execute malicious scripts in a user's session. It has yet to be assigned a CVE identifier. "The

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Zimbra crafted-email XSS payload: HTML event-handler / <details ontoggle> in mail or SOAP traffic
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable Zimbra Classic Web Client exposure (ZCS < 10.1.19)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Zimbra malicious sieve filter creating external mail-forwarding rule (post-XSS takeover) · [LLM] Zimbra webmail session mass mailbox harvest via SOAP (bulk Search/GetMsg) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Vulnerable Zimbra Classic Web Client exposure (ZCS < 10.1.19) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Zimbra Collaboration Suite hosts running a Classic Web Client build below the patched 10.1.19 release, which are exposed to the Google TAG-reported stored-XSS RCE and the closely-related exploited CVE-2025-27915. Pure exposure/attack-surface hunt keyed on the exact fixed version the vendor published. Rationale: Uses the exact vendor-published patched build (ZCS 10.1.19) from the Zimbra advisory / BleepingComputer / SecurityWeek to compute a precise sub-version exposure list; anything <10.1.19 on the 10.1 line, plus all 9.x/10.0.x, runs the vulnerable Classic Web Client. Corroborated the fixed version and Google TAG attribution across three independent write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/zimbra-urges-customers-to-patch-critical-web-client-xss-flaw/ • https://www.securityweek.com/zimbra-patches-critical-code-execution-vulnerability/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-27915
ATT&CKT1203
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Zimbra host mid-upgrade where inventory hasn't re-scanned to reflect 10.1.19
  • Zimbra deployments using only the Modern UI (not exploitable) but still flagged on version
  • Network appliance bundling an old embedded Zimbra library reported by the scanner
  • Dev/test Zimbra instance intentionally pinned to an old build
  • TVM version string with non-numeric patch suffix (e.g. 10.1.5_GA) parsed leniently
Suppression filter
| where EndOfSupportStatus != "Upgrade required" or isnotempty(SoftwareVersion)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host actually serves the Classic Web Client (/zimbra vs /modern) and the build is truly <10.1.19; cross-check against change tickets for an in-progress patch. Step 2 (contain): Prioritise internet-facing Zimbra for immediate upgrade to 10.1.19; where patching lags, disable the Classic Web Client / restrict access to the mail UI. Step 3 (hunt): For any exposed host, run UC-A and UC-D against its mailbox/audit logs for the last 30 days to rule out prior exploitation (rogue forwarding filters, SOAP harvest bursts).
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareVendor has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| extend v = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend vMajor = toint(v[0]), vMinor = toint(v[1]), vPatch = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, tostring(v[2])))
| where isnotempty(vMajor)
| where vMajor < 10 or (vMajor == 10 and vMinor < 1) or (vMajor == 10 and vMinor == 1 and vPatch < 19)
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareVendor has "zimbra" or SoftwareName has "zimbra"
| extend v = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend vMajor = toint(v[0]), vMinor = toint(v[1]), vPatch = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, tostring(v[2])))
| where isnotempty(vMajor)
| where vMajor < 10 or (vMajor == 10 and vMinor < 1) or (vMajor == 10 and vMinor == 1 and vPatch < 19)
| summarize CveIds = make_set(CveId, 20), MaxSeverity = max(VulnerabilitySeverityLevel) by DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| sort by SoftwareVersion asc

Zimbra crafted-email XSS payload: HTML event-handler / <details ontoggle> in mail or SOAP traffic AIDelivery Medium
Detects the delivery of the crafted-email XSS payload against Zimbra Classic Web Client by matching HTML5 event-handler injection (ontoggle, onerror, onload) and script/javascript: sink strings in inbound mail, ICS calendar content, or Zimbra web (SOAP/REST) traffic. Modeled directly on the CVE-2025-27915 in-the-wild payload that used a <details ontoggle=> handler inside an ICS attachment. Rationale: Payload strings (ontoggle / <details / onerror / javascript:) are taken from the confirmed CVE-2025-27915 in-the-wild ICS payload that abused the same Classic Web Client renderer this new flaw lives in; scoping to Zimbra /service/soap and /h/ endpoints keeps it specific to the mail app rather than generic web XSS. Defender left empty because Zimbra inbound mail/ICS content is not present in Advanced Hunting tables unless relayed through M365. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-27915/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/zimbra-zero-day-exploited-to-target.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1203
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing/newsletter HTML mail legitimately containing onload/onerror image handlers
  • Security-team phishing simulations carrying benign script markers
  • WAF pen-test or vulnerability scan probing the Zimbra web UI with XSS strings
  • Developers pasting HTML snippets into calendar/notes bodies
  • URL-encoded '<script' in a legitimate query parameter unrelated to exploitation
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL has_any ("/service/soap","/h/") and Message has "<details"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full request/message; confirm the event handler sits in attacker-controlled mail/ICS content (not a template) and identify the recipient mailbox and Zimbra build (cross-ref UC-C). Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the message across all mailboxes by content hash, block the sender, and force-logout/reset the affected recipient's Zimbra session. Step 3 (hunt): Run UC-A (rogue forwarding filter) and UC-D (SOAP harvest) for the recipient over the following 72h — the CVE-2025-27915 payload fired on a 60s delay and re-harvested every 3 days, so check a multi-day window.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationServiceName has "zimbra" or RequestURL has "/service/soap" or RequestURL has "/h/" or DeviceVendor has_any ("Zimbra","ModSecurity","Imperva","Barracuda","Fortinet")
| where Message has_any ("ontoggle","onerror=","onload=","onmouseover=","onanimationstart","<details","javascript:","<script")
   or RequestURL has_any ("ontoggle","%3Cdetails","%3Cscript","javascript%3A")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationServiceName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Zimbra malicious sieve filter creating external mail-forwarding rule (post-XSS takeover) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation/modification of a Zimbra mailbox filter (sieve) that redirects incoming mail to an external/personal webmail address — the exact post-exploitation action of the Zimbra Classic Web Client XSS chain, which programmatically added a filter named 'Correo' forwarding to spam_to_junk@proton.me. High-fidelity account-takeover / exfil signal. Rationale: Uses the concrete, cross-source-confirmed post-exploitation IOCs from the exploited Zimbra Classic Web Client XSS: filter name 'Correo', target spam_to_junk@proton.me, plus a generalized sieve actionRedirect-to-external-webmail heuristic so it also catches variant forwarding addresses. Zimbra sieve/filter changes are not represented in Defender AH, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/zimbra-zero-day-exploited-to-target.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-27915/ • https://securityaffairs.com/183014/hacking/zimbra-users-targeted-in-zero-day-exploit-using-icalendar-attachments.html
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1564.008
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately configuring auto-forward of their own mail to a personal Gmail/Proton account
  • Admin-created org-wide journaling/archival filter to an external partner
  • Migration tooling that recreates forwarding rules in bulk
  • Helpdesk configuring a delegate/forward for a departing employee
  • Legitimate mailing-list plumbing using redirect actions
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Correo","spam_to_junk","proton.me") or (SyslogMessage has "actionRedirect" and not(SyslogMessage has "@yourorg"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Retrieve the full sieve script and the account+client IP (oip) that created it; confirm the user did not knowingly set up forwarding and check whether the client IP matches their normal geo/device. Step 2 (contain): Delete the rogue filter, reset the account password and revoke active Zimbra sessions/tokens, and block outbound forwarding to the target address at the gateway. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the creating client IP/session to enumerate other mailboxes it touched; run UC-D for that account to gauge how much mail was already harvested, and UC-B for the delivering crafted email.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("ModifyFilterRulesRequest","CreateFilterRulesRequest","zimbraMailSieveScript","actionRedirect")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Correo","spam_to_junk","proton.me","protonmail.com")
   or (SyslogMessage has "actionRedirect" and SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)actionRedirect[^\n]{0,120}@(gmail|outlook|yandex|mail\.ru|proton(mail)?\.(me|com))")
| extend Account = extract(@"name=([^;]+);", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ClientIp = extract(@"oip=([0-9\.]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, Account, ClientIp, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Zimbra webmail session mass mailbox harvest via SOAP (bulk Search/GetMsg) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single Zimbra account/session issuing an abnormal burst of read-oriented SOAP calls (SearchRequest, GetMsgRequest, GetContactsRequest) in a short window — the automated data-harvest behaviour the XSS payload performed via the Zimbra SOAP API to siphon emails, contacts and shared folders. Threshold-based anomaly on mailbox.log SOAP activity. Rationale: Grounded in the confirmed exploitation behaviour where the Zimbra XSS payload used the SOAP API (SearchRequest/GetMsgRequest) to bulk-harvest mail, contacts and shared folders before exfiltration; the mailbox.log oip/name fields give a per-account, per-client-IP burst signal. Defender/Falcon branches pivot on the corroborated proton.me exfil/forwarding channel from the same campaign (flagged high-FP as those domains are also legitimate). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/zimbra-zero-day-exploited-to-target.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-27915/
ATT&CKT1114.002 T1119
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IMAP/EWS-to-Zimbra migration or backup tooling reading whole mailboxes
  • Mobile client initial sync of a large mailbox after re-provisioning
  • eDiscovery/legal-hold export against a mailbox
  • Zimbra desktop connector re-indexing after cache reset
  • Power user with automation/scripts against their own mailbox via SOAP
Suppression filter
| where MailboxReads > 150 and array_length(ClientIps) <= 2
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the account and client IP driving the burst; determine whether it matches a known migration/backup service or the user's normal client — a browser user-agent driving hundreds of SearchRequest/GetMsgRequest in minutes is the tell. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the account's Zimbra sessions/auth tokens and reset the password; block the client IP if external and not an expected service. Step 3 (hunt): Check UC-A for a forwarding filter planted in the same session, UC-B for the crafted email that seeded the session, and DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsRequest for outbound exfil from the user's endpoint browser following the harvest window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("proton.me","protonmail.com","mail.proton.me")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| sort by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("SearchRequest","GetMsgRequest","GetContactsRequest","SearchConvRequest")
| extend Account = extract(@"name=([^;]+);", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ClientIp = extract(@"oip=([0-9\.]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(Account)
| summarize MailboxReads = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), ClientIps = make_set(ClientIp, 5) by Account, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where MailboxReads > 150   // 150 read-SOAP ops / 5 min from one account = scripted harvest; interactive P99 < 40
| sort by MailboxReads desc
source:linux.syslog (SearchRequest OR GetMsgRequest OR GetContactsRequest OR SearchConvRequest) AND (SoapEngine OR zimbra)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/proton(mail)?\.(me|com)$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="zimbra:mailbox" OR source="*mailbox.log*") ("SearchRequest" OR "GetMsgRequest" OR "GetContactsRequest" OR "SearchConvRequest") | rex field=_raw "name=(?<zimbra_account>[^;]+);" | rex field=_raw "oip=(?<client_ip>[0-9\.]+)" | bin _time span=5m | stats count as mailbox_reads dc(_raw) as distinct_ops values(client_ip) as client_ips by zimbra_account _time | where mailbox_reads>150 | sort - mailbox_reads

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

date: 2026/05/02

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-27915", "CVE-2023-37580", "CVE-2024-27443")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-27915", "CVE-2023-37580", "CVE-2024-27443")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-27915", "CVE-2023-37580", "CVE-2024-27443")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] The Gentlemen internal recon via Advanced IP Scanner · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gentlemen initial-access CVE exposure on internet-facing edge devices · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware persistence via scheduled task named 'gentlemen*' · [LLM] GentleKiller BYOVD — vulnerable ThrottleStop.sys/ThrottleBlood.sys driver load (CVE-2025-7771) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SystemBC C2 beacon to The Gentlemen infrastructure IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] The Gentlemen anti-forensics — wevtutil clearing Security/System event logs · [LLM] The Gentlemen inhibit-recovery — Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen ransomware persistence via scheduled task named 'gentlemen*' AIInstallation High
Hunts creation/execution of any Windows scheduled task whose name matches the literal token 'gentlemen', which Unit 42 explicitly calls out as a Gentlemen RaaS execution/persistence artefact. This is article-specific because the string 'gentlemen*' is a named IOC, not a generic schtasks pattern. Rationale: Uses the exact 'gentlemen*' scheduled-task string Unit 42 flags as a high-severity SIEM alert; the literal task-name token makes this near-zero FP versus generic schtasks noise. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security/IR tool that legitimately uses the word 'gentlemen' in a task name (extremely rare)
  • Red-team or purple-team exercise emulating The Gentlemen TTPs
  • Threat-intel researcher detonating a sample in a monitored sandbox joined to the SIEM
  • Naming collision where an unrelated app packages a task string containing 'gentlemen'
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("defender-emulation.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\ImmersiveControlPanel\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full task XML (Task Scheduler Operational log / 4698 EventData) and the parent process that created it; confirm the task action points to an unknown binary in a user-writable path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable/delete the task, and preserve the referenced binary for hashing against the known Gentlemen SHA256 set. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same task name, for ThrottleStop.sys/ThrottleBlood.sys driver loads, and for outbound traffic to the SystemBC C2 IPs (45.86.230.112, 193.233.202.17, 77.110.122.137).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("ScheduledTask","gentlemen"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName has "schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "gentlemen")
    or (EventID in (4698, 4699, 4700, 4701) and EventData has "gentlemen")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventID, NewProcessName, CommandLine, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GentleKiller BYOVD — vulnerable ThrottleStop.sys/ThrottleBlood.sys driver load (CVE-2025-7771) AIInstallation High
Hunts the load or service-install of the ThrottleStop.sys (aka ThrottleBlood.sys) vulnerable driver that Gentlemen's GentleKiller framework abuses via IOCTL to terminate 400+ security processes. Article-specific because the driver filename and CVE-2025-7771 are named IOCs of this campaign's EDR-killer. Rationale: ThrottleStop.sys/ThrottleBlood.sys are the exact signed-but-vulnerable drivers GentleKiller weaponizes (same DigiCert cert, same file) — a named IOC confirmed by ESET and BleepingComputer, so a driver-load match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine overclocking enthusiast running the legitimate ThrottleStop utility on a workstation
  • Hardware/OEM diagnostic tooling that bundles ThrottleStop for CPU tuning
  • IT power-management troubleshooting on laptops
  • Security researcher testing BYOVD detections in a lab
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\ThrottleStop\" and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "TechPowerUp"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that dropped/loaded the .sys and whether it ran with SYSTEM integrity; check for concurrent EDR sensor tampering or process-termination bursts. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the driver hash via ASR/WDAC, and verify EDR tamper protection is still intact on peers. 3) Hunt: enumerate other GentleKiller variants (HexKiller, HavocKiller), the 'gentlemen' scheduled task, and any encryptor binary; scope for the same driver across all hosts via DeviceImageLoadEvents.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("throttlestop.sys","throttleblood.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceFileName has_any ("throttlestop.sys","throttleblood.sys","throttlestop","throttleblood")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen anti-forensics — wevtutil clearing Security/System event logs AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts wevtutil clearing the Security or System event logs, a defense-impairment step Unit 42 specifically recommends behavioral alerting on for Gentlemen intrusions. Scoped to the exact channels named in the article to keep it tight. Rationale: Anchors on wevtutil + the specific Security/System channels Unit 42 calls out; pairing the LOLBin with the target channel avoids the FP tail of routine wevtutil query usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing a bloated System log during troubleshooting
  • Log-management/backup scripts that rotate and clear channels after archival
  • Golden-image/build automation resetting event logs before sysprep
  • Endpoint remediation tooling that clears logs as part of cleanup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","backup-maintenance.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sysprep"
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine the parent process and user — legitimate clears come from admin sessions/scripts, malicious ones follow encryption or EDR tampering. Check for a 1102 (audit log cleared) at the same time. 2) Contain: isolate if the clear correlates with driver loads, VSS deletion, or the gentlemen task; snapshot forwarded logs before local retention is lost. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host for shadow-copy deletion, GentleKiller driver activity, and SystemBC C2 beacons.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Security","System")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "wevtutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Security","System")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen internal recon via Advanced IP Scanner AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Advanced IP Scanner, the network-mapping tool Unit 42 states Gentlemen affiliates 'frequently use' for internal reconnaissance before lateral movement. Article-specific because the tool is named explicitly as this campaign's discovery utility. Rationale: Advanced IP Scanner is named by Unit 42 as a frequently-used Gentlemen recon tool; matching on both the binary name and PE version metadata catches renamed copies. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk/IT staff legitimately inventorying a subnet
  • Network engineer troubleshooting connectivity with the same free tool
  • MSP onboarding scan of a client environment
  • Pen-test / vulnerability-assessment engagement
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("svc-netmon") and DeviceName !startswith "IT-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the executing account is IT/network staff and whether the host normally runs scanning tools; check the process's parent and preceding logons for remote-session origin. 2) Contain: if run by a non-admin/service account or off a user-writable path, isolate and reset the account's credentials. 3) Hunt: on the same host/user look for follow-on SMB access to c$/ADMIN$, the gentlemen scheduled task, GentleKiller drivers, and SystemBC C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "advanced_ip_scanner"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SystemBC C2 beacon to The Gentlemen infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the three IPs tied to Gentlemen's SystemBC SOCKS5 C2 (45.86.230.112 was the seized C2 with 1,570+ victim entries; 193.233.202.17 and 77.110.122.137 are related beacon hosts). Article-specific because these are named campaign IOCs, corroborated by Check Point's C2-server analysis. Rationale: These three IPs are named Gentlemen SystemBC C2 IOCs (45.86.230.112 was the seized C2 per Check Point); a direct IP-match on egress is high-fidelity and cheap. Cross-checked against: • https://darkatlas.io/blog/how-a-go-binary-locks-down-enterprise-networks-in-minutes-the-story-behind-gentlemen-ransomware • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1090 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP re-allocation to a benign hoster after takedown/sinkholing
  • Threat-intel platform or scanner reaching out to the IOC IP for enrichment
  • Security researcher connecting to the (now-seized) C2 for analysis
  • A honeypot/deception host deliberately talking to the IOC
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatintel-enrich.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "SANDBOX-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — SystemBC often runs from an unsigned binary in a temp/user path; validate it isn't a TI-enrichment tool. 2) Contain: block the three IPs at the firewall/proxy, isolate the beaconing host, and capture the C2 binary. 3) Hunt: expand to SystemBC SOCKS5 patterns on non-standard ports, GentleKiller driver loads, the gentlemen scheduled task, and shadow-copy deletion across the estate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("193.233.202.17","77.110.122.137","45.86.230.112")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen inhibit-recovery — Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts pre-encryption shadow-copy deletion via vssadmin or wmic, a Gentlemen impact step Unit 42 explicitly recommends behavioral alerting on. Anchored on the exact delete verbs so it fires only on destructive invocation, not on VSS listing. Rationale: Uses the exact vssadmin/wmic delete verbs Unit 42 names for Gentlemen impact; requiring both the utility and the destructive token keeps FPs to rare backup lifecycle events. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/other backup software cleaning up pre-snapshot shadow copies
  • Sysadmin manually pruning VSS storage that filled a volume
  • Windows imaging/DISM maintenance operations
  • Disk-cleanup scripts that reclaim shadow storage
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","dism.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !=~ "services.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent process — legit deletes come from services.exe/backup agents; ransomware deletes come from cmd/powershell/rundll32 chains. Look for immediately-following mass file writes. 2) Contain: isolate the host at once (this is typically minutes before encryption), kill the process tree, and freeze backups. 3) Hunt: sweep for the gentlemen task, GentleKiller drivers, wevtutil clears, and SystemBC C2; verify offline backups are intact.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName has "vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete" and CommandLine has "shadows")
    or (NewProcessName has "wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gentlemen initial-access CVE exposure on internet-facing edge devices AIExploitation High
Surfaces assets carrying the five CVEs Unit 42 lists as actively exploited by Gentlemen for initial access and privilege escalation (FortiOS, Erlang/OTP SSH, Windows SMB Client, React2Shell, ThrottleStop.sys). A vulnerability-posture hunt to prioritise patching of the specific exposures this actor weaponises. Rationale: Maps directly to the five CVEs Unit 42 lists as known-exploited by Gentlemen (initial access + priv-esc); an exposure inventory lets the SOC pre-empt the actor's entry vectors. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/unmasking-the-gentlemen-ransomware.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM reporting a CVE already mitigated by a compensating control/virtual patch
  • Version banner mismatch flagging a patched device as vulnerable
  • Decommissioned asset still present in inventory
  • A device where the vulnerable component (e.g. ThrottleStop) is not actually reachable/loaded
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by internet-exposure (IsInternetFacing) and severity — FortiOS/Erlang-SSH/React2Shell on edge first. 2) Contain: emergency-patch or virtually-patch internet-facing devices; restrict ESXi/SSH and SMB per Unit 42 guidance. 3) Hunt: for any exposed edge device, review auth logs and W3CIIS/firewall logs for prior exploitation, and monitor for follow-on Gentlemen host TTPs (gentlemen task, GentleKiller drivers, SystemBC C2).

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Non-TSDProxy backend process connecting to loopback management port 8080
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TSDProxy internal auth-token replay to localhost management API · [LLM] Unauthorized localhost call to TSDProxy /api/v1 management endpoint
TSDProxy internal auth-token replay to localhost management API AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a process invoking the tsdproxy management API on 127.0.0.1:8080 while injecting the leaked internal secret header x-tsdproxy-auth-token together with an attacker-controlled x-tsdproxy-id. These header names are unique to tsdproxy (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8) so their presence in a command line is a direct signature of the token-replay privilege-escalation exploit. Rationale: Keys on the two header names (x-tsdproxy-auth-token, x-tsdproxy-id) shown in the article's repro curl, paired with the fixed 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1 management endpoint — all strings are unique to this vuln so an in-cmdline match is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked GitLab advisory mirror and CVEReports. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A maintainer or pentester validating the GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8 fix by running the exact repro curl
  • Automated security-scanning tooling replaying the header to confirm the instance is patched
  • Internal red-team exercise reproducing the token-replay chain
  • A developer's shell-history / documentation snippet echoing the curl example that gets captured by process telemetry
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tsdproxy") and ProcessCommandLine !has "scanner" and DeviceName !in~ ("pentest-lab")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the initiating process/user; confirm the source process is a proxied backend (curl/wget/python/node/php) rather than the tsdproxy binary itself, and whether x-tsdproxy-id was set to a non-empty attacker value. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, rotate the tsdproxy internal token by restarting the service, and set identityHeaders: false pending upgrade to >=1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e. 3) Hunt: review management API access logs (/api/v1/proxies, proxy restart/pause, webhook triggers) around the event, and check other backends sharing the tsdproxy host/network namespace for the same header string.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TSDProxy Internal Auth Token Replay to Management API
id: a1f4c2e0-8b3d-4c6a-9e21-7f0d5b3a9c11
description: Detects a process injecting the tsdproxy internal secret header (x-tsdproxy-auth-token) with a spoofed x-tsdproxy-id against the 127.0.0.1:8080 management API (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/12
tags:
  - attack.t1550.001
  - attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  token:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token'
      - 'x-tsdproxy-id'
  target:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '127.0.0.1:8080'
      - 'localhost:8080'
      - '/api/v1/'
  condition: token and target
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*x-tsdproxy-auth-token* OR @process.command_line:*x-tsdproxy-id*) (@process.command_line:*127.0.0.1:8080* OR @process.command_line:*localhost:8080* OR @process.command_line:*\/api\/v1\/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/x-tsdproxy-(auth-token|id)/i
| CommandLine=/(127\.0\.0\.1:8080|localhost:8080|\/api\/v1\/)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*" OR Processes.process="*/api/v1/*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-auth-token*" OR Processes.process="*x-tsdproxy-id*") (Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:8080*" OR Processes.process="*localhost:8080*" OR Processes.process="*/api/v1/*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Unauthorized localhost call to TSDProxy /api/v1 management endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the tsdproxy management API path /api/v1/ on port 8080 arriving over loopback — the exact surface an attacker hits after stealing the forwarded token to enumerate proxies or issue admin operations (restart/pause/webhook). Because legitimate management access is Tailscale-fronted, loopback /api/v1 traffic bearing the tsdproxy identity headers is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the concrete management endpoint (/api/v1/proxies) and port 8080 named in the article's repro, scoped to loopback where the token-replay must originate; captures the network-layer view the process-cmdline UC can miss when the attacker replays from a compiled backend rather than curl. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate tsdproxy self-calls to its own management API over loopback during normal operation
  • Local health-check or monitoring probe hitting /api/v1 on 8080
  • Admin using an SSH tunnel to reach the management UI, appearing as a loopback source
  • Container orchestration readiness/liveness probes against the management port
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication has_any ("curl","python","wget","go-http-client","node") or RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT","DELETE","PATCH")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the client user-agent (RequestClientApplication) and method — a curl/python UA or a POST/PUT/DELETE to /api/v1 from loopback is high-suspicion vs the tsdproxy service's own calls. 2) Contain: block external reachability to the management port, rotate the internal token via service restart, and disable identityHeaders. 3) Hunt: correlate with process telemetry (UC token-replay cmdline) on the same host and review whether proxy configs were enumerated or services restarted/paused via the API.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DestinationPort == 8080
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/"
| where SourceIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or DestinationIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog service:tsdproxy ("/api/v1/proxies" OR "/api/v1/")
WEB

Non-TSDProxy backend process connecting to loopback management port 8080 AIExploitation Low
Surfaces a proxied backend process (curl/wget/python/node/php/shell) opening a connection to 127.0.0.1:8080 — the precondition the advisory calls out for token replay (backend must reach the management port on loopback). Pairs the leaked-token capture with the network reachability that turns it into management-API takeover. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's stated precondition ('attack requires the backend to reach 127.0.0.1:8080'); scoping to interpreter/CLI processes hitting loopback:8080 catches the reachability step even when the token itself isn't in a logged command line. Higher FP by nature, so hunting-tier. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy/GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-G936-7JQJ-MWV8
